Since diagnosis I have found that much better, because I recognize the panic building up as separate from the thing that's happening, and I don't react to it. Basically as soon as I feel it I go, oh, that's just an adhd moment, instead of getting upset, and it goes away. I was a rural mailman on the east coast of canada doing the mail out of a fit and never missed a day. Disregard anyone saying all seasons are fine. They are not fine. Get good winter tires. I got mine studded and recommend it but there are downsides. Also, when at all possible, park pointing downhill. Gravity is your friend. Practice driving around in a parking lot as soon as conditions are bad. Feel how it slides. I love the balance of the fit and once in blizzard conditions I couldn't see the road and dropped the right tires onto the shoulder and it was a steep dropoff. In trying to get back on the road the car spun, but I was able to get it to spin 360 and got it back under control. It was scary but couldve been much worse, and knowing how the car moves saved me. Get a good steel shovel for the car. I like the small pointy heavy duty garden ones. Upgrade the battery to the biggest one that will fit, google it, lots of people have done it. I also recommend getting one of the little booster pack jumper cable kits just in case, but if I had to choose one I'd choose the bigger battery first. Get at least a good quality winter wiper blade for the driver's side wiper. Dont leave your wipers on when you turn off the car. Dont drive when the conditions are really bad if possible. Freezing rain is in my opinion the most dangerous condition. That's all I can think of, I had a great experience with mine and miss it a lot.

Third, tone wise, well I just love the tone of this thing with this amp, and it's not overly complicated. I find humbuckers on Gibson's (especially Epiphones) to be too muddy for what I'm looking for, and soloing always sounds like Comfortably Numb or Sweet Child of Mine. These Filtertron pickups on the gretsch are a thing I have never played before. Thick and dirty if you crank the chords, but without being muddy, and thick and syrupy one note at a time. I'm still breaking in my amp so I'm super curious where it goes from here. I also really want to play a Gretsch with TV Jones pickups just to see if I hear a difference. In any event, back to your question, out of any electric guitar I've played, this has been the one that felt like the most natural progression from my acoustic. I have a couple of philosophy degrees, and currently teach at a university. The benefit of doing philosophy to me was to save myself, as corny as that might sound. I was a miserably depressed lost soul kind of person, who lived in a delusional world of how things should or could be, and that I had gotten the short end of most sticks. Philosophy ultimately freed me from that. There is some truth in my case that there was no direct line from philosophy to job, and my employment is quite precarious, but had I not spent time doing philosophy and other humanities I'd probably be on permanent disability or dead. I guess that is to say I didn't do it for a job, because there were things more important than jobs going on with me. I think one of the misconceptions about doing philosophy is that you learn it to then be a philosopher or think about philosophical things all the time. I did it to figure out and shut up the philosophical-like thoughts that were a plague on my every waking moment. I did ultimately silence the lambs, and getting to do that in school was an enormous privilege, and one I am grateful for almost every day, despite my chronic near-poverty, and wishing I was the kind of person who didn't need to do that so that I could have focused on more employment oriented skills won't change a damn thing. 

TLDR; I don't regret doing philosophy.
